summary: Describes how to produce digital signatures and hashes using the GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms for DNSKEY, RRSIG and DS records in DNSSEC. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC uses public keys and signatures so a resolver can check DNS data. RFC 5933 specified how to encode GOST keys, signatures, and DS digests; the RFC is now Historic and was updated by RFC 6944.

subtitle: How GOST signature and hash algorithms are represented in DNSSEC records.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC's record formats need defined algorithms and encodings for the signatures and digests used to protect DNS data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5933 specifies GOST R 34.10-2001 for DNSKEY and RRSIG records and GOST R 34.11-94 for DS digests, including the wire formats and assigned algorithm identifiers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5933 is Historic and was updated by RFC 6944. Its text records how DNSSEC algorithm 12 and digest type 3 were specified.

today: RFC 5933 is Historic and was updated by RFC 6944.

sections.title: Adding GOST Algorithms to DNSSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic keys and signatures so DNS clients can verify the authenticity and integrity of DNS data. RFC 4034 defines DNSKEY and RRSIG records and lists algorithms for those records.

RFC 5933 adds encoding rules for GOST R 34.10-2001 signatures and GOST R 34.11-94 hashes. In this document, “GOST” refers to those two algorithms; GOST 28147-89 is not used in DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how DNSSEC records carry a particular signature algorithm and hash algorithm. It adds the key and digest formats needed to represent them in DNS.

sections.title: Public Keys in DNSKEY Records
sections.content:
GOST R 34.10-2001 public keys use DNSKEY algorithm number 12. A public key is an elliptic-curve point with coordinates x and y. Its wire representation has 64 octets: the first 32 encode x and the next 32 encode y, both in little-endian order.

The RFC identifies the public-key and digest parameter sets to use. It also describes how a GOST-aware cryptographic library can receive the key in an X.509-compatible encoding by prepending a specified byte sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key is stored as two coordinates in a fixed byte sequence. The RFC specifies their order and how software can prepare the sequence for an existing library.

sections.title: Signatures in RRSIG Records
sections.content:
To create an RRSIG, the signer hashes the wire-format data of the resource-record set with GOST R 34.11-94, using the parameter set named by the RFC. It then signs that hash with GOST R 34.10-2001.

The signature contains two 256-bit values, r and s, encoded as 64 octets. The first 32 octets contain s in big-endian form, and the second 32 contain r. The RFC notes that the signature algorithm uses random data, so repeated calculations can produce different signature values.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer first creates a digest of the DNS records, then signs that digest with the private key. The RRSIG stores the signature values in the order defined here.

sections.title: DS Digests, Sizes and Registry Values
sections.content:
DS records use digest type 3 for GOST R 34.11-94. The digest is encoded in little-endian form and uses the parameter set specified by the RFC. The document lists a 512-bit public key, a 512-bit signature, and a 256-bit digest.

DNSSEC implementations may support GOST DNSKEY and RRSIG records. An implementation that supports DNSSEC with GOST must support both NSEC and NSEC3 for proving that a name does not exist. IANA added algorithm number 12 and digest type 3 as optional registry entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC assigns separate identifiers to the key-signature algorithm and the DS digest algorithm. It also states their sizes and the denial-of-existence methods a GOST implementation must support.
